subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Reading: Extensive Reading
overview: Extensive reading means reading widely on your own, for meaning and for pleasure. In this sub-strand you will choose stories, poems and simple articles that suit your age, practise ways to read more smoothly, and retell what you have read about food and health.

lessons.title: Choosing what to read
objectives: Choose a text that is interesting and mostly readable at Grade 4.
Tell a narrative, a poem, a magazine and a newspaper page apart.
Explain why reading many kinds of texts helps learning later in life.
lessons.intro: A thick book full of words you cannot say is not a brave choice. It is a frustrating one. A good independent book is interesting, mostly clear, and still gives you a few new words to keep.
lessons.notes:
### What to look for
Age-appropriate means the ideas and the words fit a learner of about nine or ten. High-interest means you actually want to know what happens. Both matter. A book can be suitable and still bore you, or exciting and still too hard.

Try this test. Read one page. If you miss only a few words and you still understand the page, the text is in a good range. If almost every line stops you, choose another text and ask your teacher for a next step, rather than pretending.

### Kinds of texts
- A narrative tells a story, with people, a place and events in order.
- A poem uses short lines, rhythm and sometimes rhyme. It can be read aloud more than once.
- A magazine often mixes short articles, pictures and interviews. A children's page is a good start.
- A newspaper reports events. Some articles are hard. Begin with a short item that has a picture and a headline you understand.

You can find these on paper or on a screen. Electronic texts are fine when a teacher or parent has opened them for you. A random link is not a library. Stay with the book, poem or site an adult has approved.

### A reason to read widely
One story can show a character choosing fruit. A poem can make you hear the words. A short article can tell you why water matters. Together they build a habit of finding things out without waiting for a lesson. That habit is part of lifelong learning: you will still need to read instructions, stories and news when nobody is marking your book.

Ask yourself three questions before you borrow a text. Do I understand most of it? Do I want to finish it? Is an adult happy for me to read it? If you can say yes, take it.

keyWords.meaning: reading many texts on your own for meaning, fluency and enjoyment
suitable for your age in words and ideas
a text that tells a story
the title in large print at the top of a news item

examples.problem: You miss about four words on a page but you understand the story. Is the book a reasonable choice?
steps: The test allows a few new words.
You still understand the page, and you can ask about those words later.
examples.answer: Yes. It is challenging enough without being too hard.

examples.problem: Sort these into narrative, poem or newspaper: a piece with short rhyming lines about mangoes; a story about a market; a report with a headline about a school garden.
steps: Rhyming lines are a poem.
Events about people at a market make a narrative.
A headline and a report belong to a newspaper.

activity.title: Build a reading choice
materials: A small pile of class readers, poems, a children's magazine or newspaper page
A device only if the teacher opens an approved text
steps: Look through three texts. Read the title and one short part of each.
Choose one you can mostly read and that you want to finish.
Tell a partner the title, the kind of text, and one reason you chose it.
Agree where an after-school reading club could meet, and what rule you will follow about approved websites.

practice.question: What does age-appropriate mean?
practice.answer: The words and ideas suit a learner of your age.

practice.question: Name two kinds of texts you can read independently.
practice.answer: Any two of: narratives, poems, magazines, newspapers, approved electronic texts.

practice.question: Why is a random link not the same as a library book?
practice.answer: A teacher or parent has not checked it. Stay with texts an adult has approved.

summary: Choose texts you mostly understand and truly want to read.
Narratives, poems, magazines and newspapers give different kinds of reading.
Wide reading is a habit you can keep after school.

lessons.title: Ways to read on your own
objectives: Use previewing, silent reading and re-reading to understand a text.
Read a familiar passage more smoothly the second time.
lessons.intro: Reading speed is not a race to skip words. Fluency means you recognise words quickly enough to keep the meaning. A few steady strategies will take you further than rushing.
lessons.notes:
### Before you read
Look at the title, the pictures and any words in bold. Ask, 'What do I think this is about?' This preview gives your mind a place to put the details.

### While you read
Read silently. Your lips do not have to move. Follow the sentences, not one lonely word at a time. When a sentence is smooth, your eyes can take in a short group of words, such as 'the ripe mangoes' or 'on the wooden table'.

If a new word appears, finish the sentence. Sometimes the next words explain it. If the meaning is still missing, underline the word or write it down and keep going, as long as you still know what is happening. Stop and ask only when the whole paragraph has become unclear.

### After a bumpy paragraph
Re-read that paragraph once, more slowly. Repeated reading of a short, familiar text is one of the best ways to become fluent. The second reading should sound calmer if you read it aloud to a partner.

### A log worth keeping
A reading log is a few lines, not a project.

- Date
- Title and kind of text
- One sentence about what happened or what you learnt
- One new word and a meaning in your own words

Ten quiet minutes a day will do more than one long session you never repeat. Use classroom readers, library books and texts your teacher has placed on a tablet. Record pleasure honestly: you are allowed to say which part you enjoyed and which part was confusing.

### Two warnings
Do not move your finger under every letter if you already know the words. The finger can slow you down. Do use it for a line you find hard, then lift it again.

Do not copy a whole page into your log. A log helps you remember. It is not a second book.

keyWords.meaning: reading words accurately and smoothly enough to follow the meaning
a quick look at the title and pictures before you read the whole text
a short record of what you read, when you read it, and one thing you learnt
to read a part again so the meaning and the sound become clearer

examples.problem: You do not know the word 'deficiency', but the next sentence says 'a lack of something the body needs'. What should you do?
steps: Finish the sentence that explains the word.
Note the meaning, then continue.
examples.answer: Take the meaning from the next sentence, write the word in your log if you wish, and read on.

examples.problem: A learner's log says only 'I read'. What should be added?
steps: A log needs the date, the title, one fact or event, and perhaps a new word.
examples.answer: The date, the title, one sentence about the text, and one new word with its meaning.

activity.title: Silent reading and a log
materials: A familiar class reader or the story in the next lesson
steps: Preview the title and any picture for half a minute.
Read silently for several minutes. Mark one new word without stopping for long.
Re-read one paragraph aloud to a partner, more smoothly than the first time.
Fill four lines of a reading log: date, title, one sentence, one new word.

practice.question: What do you look at during a preview?
practice.answer: The title, the pictures and any bold words, then you ask what the text might be about.

practice.question: Why do you re-read a bumpy paragraph?
practice.answer: The second reading makes the meaning clearer and helps you say the words more smoothly.

practice.question: Name the four lines of a simple reading log.
practice.answer: Date, title, one sentence about the text, and one new word with its meaning.

summary: Preview, read silently, and re-read parts that were unclear.
Fluency grows when you read a text more than once.
A short log helps you remember without copying the book.

lessons.title: Read, retell and give an opinion
objectives: Read a short narrative independently and retell it in order.
Share an opinion and listen to a different opinion with respect.
Use a reading strategy while you read.
lessons.intro: Retelling is the proof that you read. If the events come out in a muddle, the remedy is not a longer speech. It is another quiet look at the story.
lessons.notes:
### Market Morning
Read this narrative silently. It is written for you to manage alone.

Achieng woke early because her aunt was going to the market. She packed a bottle of drinking water and a small coin purse. At the first stall, pyramids of mangoes glowed in the sun. Next to them, a trader shook a basin of beans. 'Protein,' Achieng whispered, proud of the word from class.

Her aunt bought maize flour, the beans, a bunch of sukuma wiki and four oranges. Achieng pointed at a tall pile of sweets. 'Those are only sugar,' her aunt said gently. 'We can share one orange on the way home. The rest of the food will make a real meal.'

On the path they met a neighbour carrying a tiny baby. The aunt added an extra orange to the neighbour's bag. 'Young children need meals that suit them,' she said. 'If a child is very weak, we tell the clinic. We do not decide the illness on the road.'

At home, Achieng washed her hands, drank some water and helped sort the beans. She wrote one sentence in her reading log, then laughed, because the log was about her own morning, not about a book. 'I would still like a story tonight,' she said. Her aunt opened a thin storybook. They read it side by side.

### Retell without copying every line
A retelling needs the bones of the story.

1. Achieng went to the market with her aunt.
2. They bought maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges, and they left the pile of sweets.
3. The aunt gave an orange to a neighbour and said a weak child should be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road.
4. At home they prepared food, and later they read a book together.

### Opinions
An opinion is what you think. 'I liked the aunt's kindness' is an opinion. 'They bought beans' is a fact. Both are welcome. If a partner liked the market scene more than the ending, listen. You do not have to change your mind, and you do not have to win. Say, 'I see it differently because...' and stop there.

Independent reading matters because nobody can sit beside you for every page of your life. Each book you finish makes the next one a little easier.

keyWords.meaning: to give the main events again in order, in your own words
what you think or feel about a text, which others may not share
something the text states, which you can point to

examples.problem: Is this a fact or an opinion: 'The aunt bought beans'?
steps: Check the story.
The sentence reports an event that happened in the narrative.

examples.problem: Give one opinion about Market Morning and one reason.
steps: Choose a feeling or a judgement.
Tie it to an event so it is more than 'it was nice'.
examples.answer: I think the aunt was wise because she chose food for a meal and refused a tall pile of sweets.

activity.title: Reading club circle
materials: Market Morning or another familiar story
steps: Read the story silently. Use a preview and mark one new word.
In a circle, retell the story together, each person adding the next event.
Each learner shares one opinion. The next learner says what they heard before giving a different view.
Write a log entry. Agree to meet again as an after-school club and bring a different text next time.

practice.question: What four foods did the aunt buy?
practice.answer: Maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges.

practice.question: Why did the aunt refuse the tall pile of sweets?
practice.answer: They are only sugar. She wanted food that would make a real meal, and they could share an orange instead.

practice.question: What is the difference between a fact and an opinion in a retelling?
practice.answer: A fact is an event or detail from the text. An opinion is what you think about it.

practice.question: Why does independent reading matter after you leave class?
practice.answer: You will still need to read stories, instructions and news when a teacher is not beside you. Each text you finish makes the next one easier.

summary: Retell the main events in order and in your own words.
Label facts and opinions differently, and respect both.
Independent reading is a habit that outlasts one lesson.

quiz.question: A text is a good independent choice when
options: you know none of the words
you understand most of a page and you want to read it
quiz.explanation: Interest and a comfortable number of known words make a text suitable.

quiz.question: Short lines and rhyme usually tell you the text is
quiz.explanation: Poems are often set in short lines and may rhyme.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid a random internet link for reading practice?
options: An adult has not approved it
quiz.explanation: Use print or electronic texts that a teacher or parent has approved.

quiz.question: A preview means
options: looking at the title and pictures before you read
quiz.explanation: Previewing prepares you for the meaning.

quiz.question: Re-reading a short passage helps fluency because
options: the words become more familiar and the meaning clearer
quiz.explanation: Repeated reading of a familiar text builds smooth, accurate reading.

quiz.question: A reading log should include
options: the date, the title, one sentence and a new word
only a drawing of a sweet
quiz.explanation: A log is a short record, not a copy of the book.

quiz.question: In Market Morning the aunt said a very weak child should
options: be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road
quiz.explanation: She refused to decide an illness herself.

quiz.question: 'I liked the ending' is
options: a fact about the price of beans
quiz.explanation: It says what the reader thinks, which another reader may not share.

quiz.question: Why is wide reading useful for lifelong learning?
options: You will never need to read again
You practise finding meaning in stories, poems and information on your own
It removes every new word from English
quiz.explanation: Independent reading is a habit that continues outside class.

quiz.question: Retell one event from Market Morning in a sentence.
quiz.answer: Achieng and her aunt bought maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges, and they did not buy the pile of sweets.
quiz.explanation: A retelling gives a main event in the reader's own words.
